CHAIR ( Senator Cox ): I declare open this hearing of the Community Affairs Legislation Committee into the 2025-26 additional estimates. I begin by acknowledging the traditional custodians of the land on which we meet today and pay my respects to their elders, past and present. I extend that respect to all Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people that are here today.

The committee has fixed Thursday 9 April 2026 as the date for the return of answers to questions taken on notice. The committee would appreciate it if senators could please provide any written questions on notice to the secretariat by Thursday 19 February 2026. The committee's proceedings today will begin with the Department of Health, Disability and Ageing whole of portfolio and corporate matters. The committee will be conducting today's hearing in person and via teleconference. Under standing order 26, the committee will take all evidence in public session, and this includes answers to questions on notice.

I remind all witnesses that in giving evidence to the committee they are protected by parliamentary privilege. It is unlawful for anyone to threaten or disadvantage a witness on account of evidence given to a committee, and such action shall be treated by the Senate as a contempt. It is also a contempt to give false or misleading evidence. The Senate has endorsed the following test of relevance for questions at estimates hearings. Any questions going to the operations or financial positions of the departments and agencies which are seeking funds in estimates are relevant questions for the purposes of estimates hearings. I remind all officers that the Senate has resolved that there are no areas in connection with the expenditure of public funds where any person has the discretion to withhold details or explanations from the parliament or its committees unless the parliament has expressly provided otherwise. The Senate has also resolved that an officer of a department of the Commonwealth shall not be asked to give opinions on matters of policy and shall be given reasonable opportunity to refer questions asked of the officer to superior officers or to a minister. This resolution does not preclude questions asking for explanations of policies or factual questions about when and how policies were developed. Witnesses are reminded of the Senate's order specifying the process by which a claim of public interest immunity should be raised. I incorporate the public interest immunity statement into Hansard.

The extract read as follows—

Public interest immunity claims

That the Senate—

(a) notes that ministers and officers have continued to refuse to provide information to Senate committees without properly raising claims of public interest immunity as required by past resolutions of the Senate;

(b) reaffirms the principles of past resolutions of the Senate by this order, to provide ministers and officers with guidance as to the proper process for raising public interest immunity claims and to consolidate those past resolutions of the Senate;

(c) orders that the following operate as an order of continuing effect:

(1) If:

(a) a Senate committee, or a senator in the course of proceedings of a committee, requests information or a document from a Commonwealth department or agency; and

(b) an officer of the department or agency to whom the request is directed believes that it may not be in the public interest to disclose the information or document to the committee, the officer shall state to the committee the ground on which the officer believes that it may not be in the public interest to disclose the information or document to the committee, and specify the harm to the public interest that could result from the disclosure of the information or document.

(2) If, after receiving the officer's statement under paragraph (1), the committee or the senator requests the officer to refer the question of the disclosure of the information or document to a responsible minister, the officer shall refer that question to the minister.

(3) If a minister, on a reference by an officer under paragraph (2), concludes that it would not be in the public interest to disclose the information or document to the committee, the minister shall provide to the committee a statement of the ground for that conclusion, specifying the harm to the public interest that could result from the disclosure of the information or document.

(4) A minister, in a statement under paragraph (3), shall indicate whether the harm to the public interest that could result from the disclosure of the information or document to the committee could result only from the publication of the information or document by the committee, or could result, equally or in part, from the disclosure of the information or document to the committee as in camera evidence.

(5) If, after considering a statement by a minister provided under paragraph (3), the committee concludes that the statement does not sufficiently justify the withholding of the information or document from the committee, the committee shall report the matter to the Senate.

(6) A decision by a committee not to report a matter to the Senate under paragraph (5) does not prevent a senator from raising the matter in the Senate in accordance with other procedures of the Senate.

(7) A statement that information or a document is not published, or is confidential, or consists of advice to, or internal deliberations of, government, in the absence of specification of the harm to the public interest that could result from the disclosure of the information or document, is not a statement that meets the requirements of paragraph (1) or (4).

(8) If a minister concludes that a statement under paragraph (3) should more appropriately be made by the head of an agency, by reason of the independence of that agency from ministerial direction or control, the minister shall inform the committee of that conclusion and the reason for that conclusion, and shall refer the matter to the head of the agency, who shall then be required to provide a statement in accordance with paragraph (3).

(d) requires the Procedure Committee to review the operation of this order and report to the Senate by 20 August 2009.

(13 May 2009 J.1941)

(Extract, Senate Standing Orders)

CHAIR: I also remind senators of their obligations under the Behaviour Code for Australian Parliamentarians to treat witnesses with dignity, courtesy, fairness and respect.

Department of Health, Disability and Ageing

[09:04]

CHAIR: I now welcome Senator the Hon. Malarndirri McCarthy, the Minister for Indigenous Australians, representing the Minister for Health, Disability and Ageing. Minister, do you wish to make an opening statement?

Senator McCarthy: Good morning. I, too, would like to acknowledge the traditional owners of this land. I also thank the committee for their time in advance in terms of the estimates process today.

CHAIR: I also now welcome the Secretary of the Department of Health, Disability and Ageing, Mr Blair Comley PSM. Mr Comley, do you wish to make an opening statement?

Mr Comley : No, thank you.

CHAIR: I now call officers of the Department of Health, Disability and Ageing whole-of-portfolio and corporate matters and I invite questions. Senator Ruston.

Senator RUSTON: Good morning, Secretary and Minister. We're going to start our dance again, aren't we? Have I got any information?

Mr Comley : We have prepared to answer your questions. When you ask the questions we will answer them in the session.

Senator RUSTON: So you'll just provide the information that I've asked for when I ask the questions?

Mr Comley : In the session, yes.

Senator RUSTON: Okay. Why didn't you just provide it to me? If you've got it, there's no reason why you couldn't have provided it.

Mr Comley : We've taken a lot of time to get the information together. We've prioritised the QONs. I think I was told that in the last couple of months we've responded to over 3,000 QONs. I've just checked with my team, and all of those have been tabled today. We've responded to the QONs and we're in a position to answer your questions, I believe, when you ask them.

Senator RUSTON: All I'm saying is that, if you have the information I've asked for, it would give me the opportunity to read it, so that I'm not asking for the information but am actually able to ask you questions about the information that you give me. In a sense, by not giving me the information now, you have put another barrier in my way to actually progressing my questions. If you have the information—and you clearly do, from your statement—I'm at a loss to understand why you can't provide it to enable me to actually question you on the information, instead of spending all my time asking for the information I've already asked for and that you've just admitted that you've got.

Mr Comley : As I said, we're happy to answer the questions in the session.

Senator RUSTON: I don't know that that was my point, Secretary, but anyway—

CHAIR: Before you get started, Senator Ruston—I'm just conscious there's media in the room. If I can read this spiel before you kick off, that would be appreciated. The media have requested permission to film and take photos of proceedings, and the committee has agreed to this. I remind the media that this permission can be revoked at any time. The media must follow the direction of the secretariat staff. If a witness objects to filming, the committee will consider this request. The media are also reminded that they may not take images of senators' or witnesses' documents or of the audience. Media activity may not occur during suspensions or after the adjournment of proceedings. Copies of resolution 3, concerning the broadcasting of committee proceedings, are available from the secretariat. Senator Ruston.

Senator RUSTON: I'm loath to do this, but I feel like you've left me with no option but to read you the letter and ask you to provide the information right now. That's the choice you've left me with, I'm afraid.

'Could you please provide a list of the parliamentary committee reports focused on the portfolio, including but not limited to Senate and House of Representatives standing committee reports finalised since May 2022 that are currently awaiting a formal government response. Could you please provide me with the specific budget breakdown for each of the following measures each year over the forward estimates. In relation to expanding the bulk-billing incentive to all Australians, the Bulk Billing Practice Incentive Program, could you please provide me with the number of general practices participating in the program, by state and territory and by federal electorate, as of 31 January 2026, with a breakdown including the total number of practices that were already bulk-billed prior to 1 November 2025 and the total number of practices that have commenced fully bulk-billed services since the program began, on 1 November 2025. In relation to the average patient contribution per service for GP non-referred attendances, could you provide the average patient contribution per service for GP non-referred attendances, by federal electorate, as of 1 January 2026. In relation to aged care, could you please provide a breakdown by state and territory and by federal electorate of Support at Home packages released since 1 November 2025, including the number of packages released at each support level; the number of packages assigned and allocated to individuals at each support level; the number of individuals who were approved for a package at one support level but were allocated a package at a lower support level, broken down by approved level and allocated level, and the average wait times between approval and allocation for these individuals; the number of packages released as interim 60 per cent packages, broken down by approved level, and the average waiting time between approval and allocation of their full package; the timeline for the additional 43,000 Support at Home packages scheduled to be released between 1 January and 30 June 2026; the number of Australians on the National Prioritisation System as of 31 January 2026—and please provide a national figure as well as one broken down by federal electorate; the latest number of Australians waiting to be assessed under the Single Assessment System, aged care assessment teams and regional assessment teams as of 31 January 2026; the number of Australians currently receiving the Commonwealth Home Support Program as of 31 January 2026; and the number of Australians currently waiting to receive a Commonwealth Home Support Program package as of 30 January 2026.'

Mr Comley : We are ready to answer all those questions. Chair, I'll just take your guidance. We're in the cross-portfolio part of the estimates. Many of those questions go to the specifics that would be handled under outcome 1 or outcome 2—in fact outcome 3, because it's aged care. Do you want us to answer those questions now, or do you want us to wait until we've moved out of cross-portfolio and into those sessions?

CHAIR: I think they are relevant within the particular outcome areas. Just to clarify, I think the preference would be to ask those within those areas. I will allow some general questions. Getting into the granular detail of what it is that Senator Ruston might be looking for, in relation to issues that may require some more conversation, is much more detailed. This area is really more for corporate matters, I would think, and high-level conversation, rather than getting into the detail of what I think Senator Ruston has outlined in that letter. My preference would be to move through this area quite quickly. I have relayed previously to other members of the committee, in the shaping of this program, that we could spend more time within the outcome areas. So I would ask for the indulgence of other committee members. If we move through this quite quickly, we could get into having more time for the answering of the questions by Senator Ruston as she's outlined in her letter.

Senator RUSTON: Thank you very much, Chair. Obviously I respect your direction, so could I ask, Mr Comley, that at the start of each of the sections the information be tabled for all committee members to see so that we have it at the start of each section—obviously the officials will be here for those sections—in response to the chair's suggested direction. Quite frankly, this looks like you are trying not to answer the questions. Now, I'm not saying you are—I'm just saying that's what it looks like. Have all of the questions that we've put on notice so far been responded to?

Mr Comley : I've been advised that all the QONs have been responded to.

Senator RUSTON: When was that? They certainly weren't all up yesterday.

Mr Comley : I'm not sure exactly when the last one was.

Ms Balmanno : The last of them have been tabled this morning.

Senator RUSTON: How many were tabled this morning?

Ms Balmanno : Seventeen.

Senator RUSTON: How many have been—

Ms Balmanno : About 3½ thousand.

Senator RUSTON: So the whole 3½ thousand—wow!

Ms Balmanno : They've all been done.

CHAIR: That just proves how quickly they've been working.

Senator RUSTON: Okay. Well, I can assure you—

CHAIR: There's been an excessive amount of questions on notice.

Senator RUSTON: I can assure you, Chair, that an excessive amount of those questions didn't belong to me. Mine were—

CHAIR: Well, you might want to chat to your colleagues about that.

Senator RUSTON: I have no control over my colleagues. Thank you. I will get someone in my office to go and dig out the answers to those questions.

Ms Balmanno : We have copies of the most recent ones, if there are some you'd like us to table, knowing that they were new.

Senator RUSTON: Are they uploaded?

Ms Balmanno : I believe they are, yes.

Senator RUSTON: The only reason I'm saying that is because, for much of the information that I've requested in my letter, there's a lot of crossover with what was in the answers to those questions.

Ms Balmanno : Yes.

Senator RUSTON: So, maybe, at last, I actually do have the answers to them.

Ms Balmanno : One of the questions in your letter also went to parliamentary inquiry responses, so we have that answer for you in this session, if you like.

Senator RUSTON: That's great. I don't want it read to me; I'd actually like it.

Ms Balmanno : It's very short.

CHAIR: Are you happy for them to table that so that you—

Senator RUSTON: Yes.

CHAIR: I can instruct the secretariat to give you a copy. Is that what we're suggesting?

Senator RUSTON: Yes.

CHAIR: I'm just trying to get some efficiency in this.

Senator RUSTON: When you say it's only very short, does that mean that there are not very many inquiries that haven't—

Ms Balmanno : Correct.

Ms Laffan : That's correct. I'm just flagging that there are only four responses outstanding.

Senator RUSTON: What are they to?

Ms Laffan : They are responses to inquiries into the state of diabetes mellitus in Australia in 2024, the Public Governance, Performance and Accountability Amendment (Vaccine Indemnity) Bill 2023, the Aged Care Bill 2024 provisions and the health impacts of alcohol and other drugs in Australia.

The assessment workforce undertakes the assessment, then an algorithm is run—the integrated assessment tool classification algorithm—and what that does is use a set of rules to objectively assign each participant to a funding class based on their clinical characteristics. It does that because we want to make sure that people who have the same or a similar level of acuity of needs conditions are matched with similar levels of support so you don't have the two folks that you've mentioned in your case study receiving one level and then two folks who are in exactly the same position receiving something markedly different. CHAIR: Senator Ananda-Rajah.

Senator ANANDA-RAJAH: With regard to the new aged-care facility in Palmerston, Northern Territory that the Prime Minister announced at the end of January, how many extra beds will there be, and what will be the additional capacity of this facility for Greater Darwin?

Ms Milfull : Essentially, it's a new 120-bed residential care home, and the aim is for it to be built over the next 24 to 36 months after approvals. The aim is to meet the diverse needs of the Greater Darwin community, including obviously Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people and people with dementia. One of the key things is that it would be built in line with new dementia design principles. The intention is also that there will be a memory support unit. CHAIR: Senator Pocock.

Senator DAVID POCOCK: I have questions on respite care.

Ms Milfull : Are they about the commitment?

Senator DAVID POCOCK: I'll get to that. Firstly, people have been reporting to me that they can no longer access Burrangiri aged-care respite in the ACT using their Support at Home package. They're saying that they could access it when they were on a home-care package, but now they're on a Support at Home package they can't. I'm interested in what's going on there.

Ms Milfull : I'm happy to start, and then my colleagues might jump in. My understanding is that, essentially, from a Commonwealth aged-care perspective, Burrangiri is largely operated on a private basis. They had these services available both before and after 1 November. They were private fees. I think what has changed is before 1 November some people were using their home-care package fees to, if you like, supplement those private fees. That's the difference between before 1 November and after. But, Greg Pugh, you might want to add to the post 1 November situation.

Senator DAVID POCOCK: Everyone was told that they would be no worse off. Why could they access respite care when they had a home-care package, and now that they've got a Support at Home package they can't? This is despite the fact, in the inquiry we did into the transition, we were told that people wouldn't even notice, that it was just a new system and that things would actually be better. What's going on here? You'd know how hard respite is to access in the ACT.

Mr Pugh : There are probably two parts to your question. The first part is around the policy. You are right that the Support at Home service list does give access to the following respite types. It gives you access to flexible respite, which gives you support and assistance in an older person's home during the day or overnight. And there is also community and centre based respite, which provides support through small day outings or structured group activities. The service type cottage respite is not available under the Support at Home program; however, it is accessible under the Commonwealth Home Support Program. If you are in the Support at Home program, you can still access cottage respite simultaneously by getting it with CHSP, and you can do that by getting a referral for CHSP cottage respite. You can do that by either getting a support plan review undertaken or getting an urgent referral for CHSP cottage respite, and you do that by contacting the My Aged Care contact centre. So it is a change, but the access to the cottage respite service is still there. I think there's a secondary issue, which Ms Milfull was just going through, around access in the broad once you're approved for it.

Senator DAVID POCOCK: So how are these Canberrans no worse off?

Ms Trainor : As I think we talked about at the last hearings, the no-worse-off principle is specific to the amount of contribution in dollars that a person makes to their care. At the announcement of the reforms on 12 September 2024, Minister Wells noted a no-worse-off principle will provide certainty to people already in aged care and they won't make a greater contribution to their care. So it's a very specific principle and is not about all matters to do with aged care around service provision and what may or may not be on service lists.

Senator DAVID POCOCK: From talking to Canberrans, that's not what they were hearing. They were hearing they'd be no worse off. I think that, when you talk to older people, that's about the services that they receive. It sounds like there's a lot of hoops to jump through now if you do actually want to go to Burrangiri on your Support at Home packages. They have to get access assessed through CHSP currently?

Mr Pugh : That's right.

Senator DAVID POCOCK: But isn't the government shutting down CHSP?

Mr Pugh : The commitment to transition the CHSP is currently committed to do so no sooner than first July 2027. As we gave evidence at the inquiry hearing last week, you know, there is absolute merit in retaining a whole raft of either fee for service or block funded programs. We know cottage respite is a great service for people, and so that is absolutely forming part of our consideration around what the future of that service looks like post 2027.

Senator DAVID POCOCK: Why were these changes made? We're having a conversation about hospital funding and just how many people are unnecessarily in hospital beds in this country. We're also having a conversation about productivity and the need to improve productivity. It seems like we've come up with a system that's going to make it harder for people to get respite and is less productive, because you've got to jump through all these ridiculous hoops. What's the intent behind this? Is it to reduce the number of people going into respite? Is it to save the Commonwealth money? Why was this decision taken?

Mr Pugh : There are a couple of things on that. It's not about saving money at all. The Support at Home service list, as I said, still gives you access to flexible respite and community incentive based respite through the broad consultations that were undertaken on the Support at Home service list that went on for multiple years before it was agreed by government Cottage respite did not feature because there was a view that it would be more readily maintained and accessible through the Commonwealth Home Support Program. So that was the way that the distinction was made between the two. Having said that, we're not deaf to the calls of the community. We understand that people would like to be able to access cottage respite either through using their Support at Home funding or being able to access it more in general. This forms part of our ongoing review processes into what's on the Support at Home service list.

Senator DAVID POCOCK: One of the things I hear from older Australians and particularly from carers is just how complex this whole thing is to navigate. Why have you decided for cottage respite to be assessed through CHSP when you've committed to ending CHSP in July next year? Why have you made that decision to shift it to a service that you're going to abolish anyway, and what happens after that?

CHAIR: The opening statement is quite clear about asking officials to give their opinion about why things are happening. I'm trying to do is be helpful about this. I know what you're asking and I think officials are capable of answering that question. I think we just tread the line very carefully in relation to asking them about what their intention is or what their opinion is in relation to why these things are happening. I would ask that possibly those questions about government and decisions be directed to the minister at the table rather than to officials. I just caution you in thinking about who you're asking the question and in what frame.

Senator DAVID POCOCK: Thanks, Chair. To be clear, I don't want any opinions here. Why did you do that, and then what happens after July next year?

Mr Pugh : I am going to throw—

Ms S Stewart : Sorry Mr Pugh, but I want to clarify something, Senator, which was your characterisation about what's happening on 1 July 2027, if that's OK. I think you're using terminology around 'abolishing' and something ending and, before Mr Pugh went into the detail, I wanted to say that the actual commitment and what the government stated a couple of years ago was that the CHSP will move into Support at Home no earlier than 1 July 2027. Senator DAVID POCOCK: So CHSP will continue, or does it end next July?

Ms S Stewart : That's a decision for government.

Senator DAVID POCOCK: They've already said it'll—

Ms S Stewart : It says 'no earlier than'. It doesn't say 'on that date' or 'by that date'; it says 'no earlier than 1 July 2027'. That is what the government has committed to.

Senator DAVID POCOCK: But their intention is to move it into Support at Home.

Ms S Stewart : The government has made a commitment that that it will move into Support at Home but not in terms of the details of that and not with the timeframe.

Senator DAVID POCOCK: I feel like this is semantics.

CHAIR: Let Ms Stewart answer.

Mr Comley : I don't think it's semantics. Senator DAVID POCOCK: Thank you. And I'll come to consultation later on. Mr Pugh, did you want to—

Mr Pugh : I was basically going to say the same thing that Ms Stewart said and refer to my previous statement that we know the importance of cottage respite ongoing. It's a broad statement to say that CHSP is being shutting down and that cottage respite is just going to be eliminated. I want to make the point that that is not the case or is not forming part of our advice. I will just ask Ms Atkinson to supplement.

Ms Atkinson : I will refer back to some of the evidence I provided at the Senate inquiry on Friday. Senator DAVID POCOCK: Thank you. I can see what carers are saying about just how complicated this is to try to deal with when you also have a job and other commitments. To be clear: you have to go through CHSP now to get cottage respite, but, when CHSP transitions into Support at Home no earlier than July 2027—at some future date the decision of government—you'll have to be assessed through Support at Home?

Mr Pugh : That remains to be a decision of government. However, just taking in your points around if there is complexity around the way that it's currently working, we would obviously want to move to a system that is as easy for people to access as they possibly can. So there's no decision, but that's the broad principle that's guiding our thinking and advice.

Senator DAVID POCOCK: So what do I tell the Canberrans who are telling me that they can't access Burrangiri with their Support at Home package but they could with their home-care package?

Mr Pugh : I think it's a matter of ringing My Aged Care, getting an urgent referral and getting access to cottage respite that way.

Senator DAVID POCOCK: Thank you. I'll pass that on. I'll go to consultation and the $10 million for respite earmarked for the ACT, which I really thank the government for. It's a really important investment. When we're talking about Burrangiri, this is half of the ACT's respite beds, so it's incredibly consequential for Canberrans. Ms Milfull : I can certainly provide you with a full list on notice. I've attended some of those meetings, so I could certainly say, from memory, Goodwin and Warrigal, for example. Senator DAVID POCOCK: Thank you. That'd be great. One of the other things which I was pretty disappointed to read in the QON goes to the secretary's point around consultation. Ms Milfull : At this point of this journey, I think we have been consulting on some quite technical details with ACT Health and Community Services Directorate and those providers. I think it's been very much focused on that infrastructure solution and making sure those beds are available so, as you say, we don't end up in a situation that's worse. I think the department, the government and certainly the ACT government are really cognisant of the need to continue to work together. This is not the end of the story. This is solving one plank of that respite problem. But I know I meet, personally, regularly with the directorate. We're very keen to continue that work together and make sure we're also communicating together with the community. Senator DAVID POCOCK: Surely it should be the other way around. Senator DAVID POCOCK: There's a lot of anxiety around the looming June 2027 shutdown of Burrangiri, so maybe you could provide us with some information about what options you're exploring and whether or not there's a firm commitment for there to be no loss of beds mid next year with Burrangiri shutting down.

Ms Milfull : It's probably a question for government, but I'd just say I think we are very close at getting to a position that, if you like, government is comfortable with, so I would expect there would be some more information that we could release reasonably soon that, hopefully, will give community an idea of the proposed way forward, and then those further discussions can also happen.

Senator DAVID POCOCK: I'm keen to follow up on this, but I will pass the call. Thank you.

Senator RUSTON: With the greatest amount of respect, that sounds like the greatest load of rubbish I have ever heard in my life. You've promised 83,000 packages. Senator RUSTON: Thank you, Chair. I understand. In terms of this year's MYEFO, it shows in the papers that there is a saving of $80 million over two years from 2025-26 through reprioritising unspent funds in the Commonwealth Home Support Program growth funding grant opportunity to other aged-care services. I'm just interested to understand, given the incredibly high level of demand, what the reason behind the $80 million underspend that has been reprioritised in MYEFO was.

Ms Atkinson : Commonwealth Home Support Program is a grant program. It provides block funding to a range of different organisations across the country to deliver a whole range of different services. Because it's a block funded program, it's not as responsive to supply and demand as, for example, an entitlement based or package based program might be. That means government has to plan for how much funding they're going to put into each and every funding agreement for each provider, each region and each service type. Sometimes that planning isn't 100 per cent 12 months down the track. It's one of the downsides of that model of funding.

What it looks like in practice is that in the Commonwealth Home Support Program there are some areas where we hear that providers are not able to service all the clients who are knocking on their door. There are some areas and some service types where providers are not able to service all the clients that are knocking on their door, and there are some areas and some service types where providers are not able to spend all the funding that has been allocated to them. For the latter type, that funding will be returned to government.

Senator RUSTON: If I could stop you there, sorry: I understand that the allocation of grant funding is not uniform across the landscape. That makes perfect sense. But I'm keen to understand: the money that's been reallocated has been reallocated to other programs, not back within the CHSP program, I gather from that?

Ms Atkinson : That's correct, and that's why it appears as a measure.

Senator RUSTON: Sure. I get that. But what I don't understand—well, maybe I should ask you: my understanding is that there is way more demand for CHSP services if you look at them at the macro level than is currently being delivered on. Whilst I understand that there may be places where that funding may not be able to be expended for whatever reason, why wasn't that $80 million redirected to other CHSP services that were finding that their demand exceeded their capacity to supply?

Ms Atkinson : It's a fair question, and I guess, to take it to an even more macro level, it would be fair to say that there is increasing demand on the aged-care system, period, and government needs to make difficult decisions around the allocation of funding when faced with a proportionately small underspend compared with the total of that program, and it is $7.2 billion over two years. That $80 million is proportionally very small. The government redeploys that funding within that program. There would be a 12- to 18-month lead time in which to do that, because it would need to be done through a grants round. So, government needs to make difficult decisions—

Senator RUSTON: Could I ask you, then: on the basis that you just said it would need to be reallocated within the 18 months, I'm assuming you mean by 1 July 2027?

Ms Atkinson : No, what I mean is that it would take a period of time to reallocate that funding, so—

Senator RUSTON: Why?

Ms Atkinson : Because you need to go through an appropriate Commonwealth grants round process in order to reallocate that funding, and it needs to be in line with the Commonwealth grant guidelines. It's the way the program is structured. We don't just pour money out the door willy-nilly; it needs to go through a process, and that has to have probity in place and people need to be given the opportunity to apply for that funding—

Senator RUSTON: Don't you heat-map the country and work out where there is the greatest need? Do you not have any idea of where the demands for services are?

Ms Atkinson : We have some idea of where the demands for services are, yes. Do we have a perfect heat map of demand for services? No, we don't. That goes to some of the evidence I provided earlier today around the imperfect nature of the data we're dealing with in this program. We aren't able to follow a client's journey from assessment through to service provision. So, what we do, or have done historically, when deploying growth rounds—and this is something that governments have done, and a $100 million growth round was deployed, the funding went out, last financial year—we look at relativities across different service types and service areas and we look at where those relativities are higher in a mismatch between number of referrals going out and number of referrals being taken up.

That gap is always going to be an overestimate, because when somebody gets assessed for a Commonwealth Home Support Program they may get a whole range of codes for different service types, and they may choose to take up only some of those. They may wish to take one up but are not able to access that service in their region because of service availability. At the present moment we don't have the ability to disaggregate those issues, so we have to operate broadly on estimates. We look at those relativities. I would love a heat map of where the supply and demand for CHSP are, but we don't have that at present.

Senator RUSTON: Okay. Thank you. Did we manage to get any data around what had happened in terms of new builds in the last six months of 2025?

Ms Harper : The team are working away on that request. Regrettably, I'm not going to be able to provide it today, so I will need to take that on notice, if that's okay.

Senator RUSTON: Thank you very much. I understand. It obviously is a huge issue, going forward. Ms S Stewart : I think the first thing that we require is an agreed definition of 'delayed discharge' of older people across Australia, and then the states and territories would provide data against that definition.

Senator RUSTON: So you don't have the national figures? You can't provide me with national figures because you're worried about the definitional issue?

Ms S Stewart : I wouldn't say I'm worried about the definition. It needs to have a definition agreed to by states and territories in the Commonwealth, and then that data is collected against that definition.

Senator RUSTON: Why are they taking so long to do that? I would have thought, given the noise that we've heard out of the states and territories in recent times, they'd be pretty eager to get a definition.

Mr Comley : We've only just signed a National Health Reform Agreement.

Senator RUSTON: I think we noticed that.

Mr Comley : Yes. And—

Senator RUSTON: I'll ask you about that in the next section.

Mr Comley : That was in cross-portfolio.

Senator RUSTON: Bad luck! You're still here.

Senator RUSTON: Okay. I think, at the last estimates, it was roughly estimated that there were about 3,000 older Australians across the country that were—

Mr Comley : We wouldn't endorse any particular figure because we just do not think there's a robust definition that would allow you to determine that.

Senator RUSTON: Nonetheless, there's not nobody in a hospital bed. In terms of the National Health Reform Agreement, as an example, clearly this has been a really big issue when it comes to the agreement because, obviously, the states and territories have been very harsh in their criticism of the fact that older Australians were causing the bed block in their hospitals, and obviously there's a cost associated with that. Senator RUSTON: Does the department have any capacity at all to do an assessment of the clinical and health outcomes for those older Australians who are stuck in hospital beds because they can't get access to home-care packages or there's not a place in a residential facility for them, or aren't they your problem?

Mr Comley : The others may want to comment. We actually work in a very active case management way with the states and territories and a range of locations to try to find solutions to this. This was during a time, as you would recall, when the risk-benefit of providing a provisional authorisation for that vaccine was high. Since then we have undertaken a transition of that vaccine through to a full market authorisation. As Dr Noja has highlighted, we do have a fairly robust postmarket surveillance process in place, so if there are problems with the curette—if there is any propensity to be infected, or it is unable to be sterilised, or if they deform or bend and snap when they're being used—we are able to pick up these safety signals and respond to them with appropriate market action.

Senator HODGINS-MAY: I'm just trying to understand—one woman was told by the TGA that sharp curettes cannot be a higher class than class 1 because they're not long-term implants. By that logic, you know, any sort of tool used surgery could also be classified as class 1 because it's not implanted.

Dr Noja : I might ask my colleague to talk to the approvals process.

Prof. Lawler : While Mr Jamieson is approaching the table, I'll clarify that we have separate areas within the TGA that go to market authorisation and postmarket surveillance. We are in constant conversation because, obviously, we need to balance the risk of devices across the lifecycle. But, in terms of the classification of medical devices, I'll ask Mr Jamieson to comment.

Mr Jamieson : To your question around the classification of medical devices, we have a principles based set of classification rules in the legislation, so it's established in law. You are quite right that the principles for the classification rely on things like the level of invasiveness of the device and the duration of use of the device. So, under that basis, that's what's behind that statement.

Senator HODGINS-MAY: By that logic, a chainsaw used in surgery could be classified as class 1 because it's not implanted. It seems a bit—

Mr Jamieson : I think the other part is the classification of a device is not a measure of its level of significance in the health system. It is the level of scrutiny applied before the product is approved. It's not a measure of the level of significance or scrutiny applied after the product is approved for sale.

Dr Noja : If I may jump in—in the postmarket space, when we receive signals, sometimes when we assess the information around the device, we do look at the classification and assess if it's still fit for purpose. As we know with urogynecological mesh, part of what we did there was actually up classify those products, because we found that the classification for those products wasn't appropriate relative to the risk of using those products. So classifications can change, if we feel that the evidence is showing that it is necessary to do so. When it comes to these sharp curettes, we've not seen as yet that there is evidence to suggest that because of the significant impact of clinical practice on women who have Asherman's syndrome.

Senator HODGINS-MAY: Do you expect that this will be kept on the agenda of the advisory group?

Dr Noja : I can't comment on the advisory group, but, in respect of what the TGA is doing more broadly, we do continue to monitor and check for signals in respect to Asherman's. We do have a very robust postmarket system. We receive over 20,000 signals that we regularly assess, and we ensure that we are directing our resourcing to where the highest risk is for the Australian public.

Prof. Langham : In answer to your question about the advisory group, we absolutely undertake to report any changes back to members as they happen. Occasionally, we'll get specific external groups in to speak to us again about any of their changes that they may have had so that the whole of the working group can keep up to date with any changes.

Senator HODGINS-MAY: I'll go back to the minister. Speaking of listening to women, as you've said that you're doing, women affected by Asherman's syndrome have been calling for years for public and clinical guidelines on when uterine curettes may be used, the risks and alternative treatment options. RANZCOG finally released updated miscarriage guidelines in May 2025 that included this advice. However, they have not provided any public guidelines or guidelines for clinicians, as far as we're aware, on the use of uterine curettes in the postpartum period. Experts say that women two to four weeks postpartum are 25 to 30 per cent more likely to develop Asherman syndrome or haemorrhage or to suffer uterine perforation as a result of curette misuse. Would you say that that is enough evidence to prompt the government to step in and require or develop clinical and public guidelines?

Senator Green: Thank you for raising it. We certainly do listen to women, and we also listen to the experts around the issue of clinical guidance. I'm certainly not a clinical expert at all, so I can't give you advice about what the next steps would be. But the officials have stepped you through the process that is being undertaken and the continual monitoring of any devices that might be considered by the TGA.

Senator HODGINS-MAY: I have no further questions. Thank you for your time.

Senator ROBERTS: I'll continue with the TGA, please. As more and more harm emerges from the COVID jabs, and I note the TGA is now talking about harm exceeding benefit for young people, the long process of scientific inquiry into the clinical trials has started, with the purpose of to establish how the results from the clinical trial could vary so badly from actual results. I've provided you with one copy of a very long document titled 'The assessment of methodological methological practices implemented in Pfizer's COVID-19 mRNA vaccine trials with respect to good clinical practice'. I've also sent the secretariat an electronic copy. I'm not seeking to table it. The paper shows 'multiple methodological bias and major violations to good clinical practice'. When was the last time you revisited your processes that saw a product approved that should never have been approved?

Prof. Lawler : Thank you very much for that question. Obviously, as a contemporary regulator, we are constantly reviewing not only our processes but the therapeutic goods that we've approved and authorised. We've had conversations here on a number of occasions around the pharmacovigilance and postmarket surveillance activities that we undertake. You and I have both said the same thing—that it's important that, as robust and reliable evidence and scientific advancement comes up, as we understand more and more, as our understanding evolves, around the process that governs vaccination, the human body's response to infection and the human body's response to vaccination, so should our regulatory decision making. It does. We've had the conversation previously around the difference between science and pseudoscience—that is, it is important when information is published to view that in the appropriate context. The article that you've provided, I think it's really important to understand where that sits. It is challenging to draw strong scientific conclusions from the article you provided. It has invalid epidemiological comparisons. It uses evidence selectively. The toxicology in it is speculative and is not supported by evidence. This article would not survive peer review in a mainstream journal.

What we do in our scientific assessment is we look to the rigour of the science. We don't look to the outcomes; we look to the rigour. There are a number of issues with this article. The methodology itself is flawed. It doesn't contain independent peer review. It doesn't contain conflict-of-interest disclosures, which themselves would disqualify it from publication in a mainstream, credible review. It was released by an organisation called the Children's Health Defence, which we know is a political advocacy organisation with an explicit antivaccination agenda. The challenge also is that the authors themselves don't have expertise in vaccine pharmacology or regulatory toxicology or clinical immunology, so these are really hard things to reconcile. I know you introduced the document by saying that it has 200 peer review papers, but the challenge is that they are selectively chosen on the basis of satisfying a predetermined outcome. If I can give you one example, in 2025, a large Danish nationwide cohort study of almost 1.3 million children found no evidence supporting an increased risk for autoimmune, atopic or allergic or neurodevelopmental disorders in early childhood.

Senator ROBERTS: Is this an order?

Prof. Lawler : Sorry, Senator, this is actually important to the document that you've highlighted. From cumulative exposure to vaccines containing aluminium, this article does not mention it. Now, it may not agree with it, but it does not mention a study that had 1.2 million—

Senator ROBERTS: I asked you a question about when was the last time you revisited your processes that saw a product approved that should never have been approved? When was the last time?

Prof. Lawler : I answered at the beginning of the process that we are continually reviewing our processes.

Senator ROBERTS: In terms of the products that have failed in the marketplace?

Prof. Lawler : Can I have an example, because I'm not sure what you mean by that.

Senator ROBERTS: You're infallible processes failed when it came to sunscreen, didn't it? A CHOICE investigation, and I must compliment CHOICE, found 16 of the 20 sunscreens tested failed, only delivering an SPF of four or five instead of 50. Did the TGA actually test these products before you licence them, or did you take the manufacturer's word for it again?

Prof. Lawler : Well, thank you very much for that question. I'm just asking Mr Avinash Clarke, who heads up our complementary and over-the-counter medicines branch, to join us. We've highlighted to you previously that we regulate proportionately based on the risk presented by the product, so there are different requirements on products and that goes to pre and postacceptance testing. As you've mentioned, we have taken on board the findings of the CHOICE article. We've been in conversations with sponsors and other regulators and we are revisiting our processes. I'll ask my colleagues.

Senator ROBERTS: I'll just point out there's a list of 16 here. I won't go through the names because it'll take me all day to go through the names. It says: first, voluntarily recalled all batches—listing cancelled from the register; second also recalled—cancelled; third, voluntarily recalled—cancelled from register; fourth, voluntarily recalled; another, voluntary recalled; recalled; recalled, recalled or paused; recalled or paused; recalled or paused; recalled or paused; recalled; sales paused voluntarily for retesting; sales paused or removed; sales paused, linked and affected—16.

Prof. Lawler : You asked us when we last revisited a decision that we've made and you've just given us a list of 16 times when we have. So what we've done is respond to market issues. We've responded to—

Senator ROBERTS: You approved these products.

Prof. Lawler : You've asked us when we have gone back and reviewed decisions that we've made and you've read us out a list of 16 times when we have.

Senator ROBERTS: Thanks to CHOICE.

Prof. Lawler : You asked us when we last made a decision and we've reviewed that, then you've read out for us a list of the times that we have. Part of the process that we undertake, as any regulator does undertake, is that we have a complementary pre and postmarket process so that, when concerns arise, we respond with appropriate regulatory actions. We have a regulatory, if you like, pyramid or regulatory triangle, where we work through education and guidance, all the way up to compliance, and we review our processes. That's what we're currently doing. If you have an interest in what we're doing with that, I'm more than happy to throw to my colleagues.

Senator ROBERTS: Well, you acknowledged CHOICE, so would you have done it without CHOICE sticking its nose in?

Prof. Lawler : As I've said, Senator, if you're interested in what we're doing in response to that, I'm happy to call on my colleagues.

Senator ROBERTS: I appreciate the outcome was 12 products being removed or recalled with SPF as low as 4—advertised 50—which shows CHOICE was correct. Was 12 the final tally of products withdrawn or recalled, and did inquiries extend to other brands? There having been a failure to correctly supervise something parents use to protect their children, I'm wondering how far the inquiries went. Now maybe they can talk.

Mr Henderson : Thank you for the question, Senator. I might also clarify, just based on the previous line of questioning. Sunscreens are captured under our listed medicines framework, so they do not undergo a premarket assessment by the TGA. However, we do have in place postmarket compliance activities that we look for and identify where there are concerns or issues with those listed medicines, such as adverse events being reported to the TGA but, importantly, also signals that we receive from research organisations or consumers or generally on social media. Senator ROBERTS: So they do the research for you.

Mr Henderson : from these CHOICE investigations as one of those signals.

CHAIR: Senator Roberts, can we just let the witness finish his evidence, please.

Mr Henderson : So we have taken these CHOICE findings very seriously. That was that sunscreen Ultra Violette that had SPF claims of 50 but was tested by CHOICE to have SPF claims below 4. Senator ROBERTS: Thank you.

Mr Henderson : But I can assure you, Senator, as well, that our investigations are ongoing and we continue to investigate not only those sunscreens that were identified by CHOICE but a number of different sunscreens.

Ms Jin : I will just expand on what Professor Lawler mentioned earlier. The TGA does have an ongoing program to inspect manufacturers regularly. We look at a number of elements. Senator ROBERTS: Thank you.

Mr Clarke : I'll add to that as well. In our compliance work related to sunscreen, one of the things we look specifically at is the product on the shelf—what has actually been tested for. Senator ROBERTS: Sunscreen manufacturers—did you take any action against them? They deceived you. They've got an SPF of four or five when they're advertising 50.
