Senator RUSTON: So I suppose part of this is around people understanding and getting the information. It may not be your issue, Professor Lawler. It may be the department's. I don't know. But what is being done to improve the awareness amongst patients and clinicians around the potential complications and impact of D&C procedures, including awareness of Asherman's syndrome?

Prof. Lawler : I think this is an important reflection of the key role of the TGA in working with clinical stakeholders. As has been mentioned previously today, we have representation on the Women's Health Product Working Group, which has key clinical leadership organisations within it, including the college of obstetricians and gynaecologists, the ANMF, the Australian College of Rural and Remote Medicine and also the Consumers Health Forum. So we endeavour to ensure that there is an understanding within both clinical and consumer bodies to that extent. As has also been mentioned, we've been doing some work with the Commission on Safety and Quality and Health Care on clinical guidelines and standards and the understanding of that. It's important to note as well that part of our role is to encourage and improve the facility for patients and health practitioners to report when they have had negative experiences or adverse events related to medical devices. That goes to our ability to raise the understanding of what concerns may be there.

Senator RUSTON: Sure. This question is probably one for the department. Obviously there is a risk of Asherman's as a result of these particular treatments. So I'm interested to understand: has there been any action taken through whatever mechanisms are available to the government around diagnosis and treatment of Asherman's syndrome becoming more accessible or making diagnosis more enabled and treatment of Asherman's more accessible as a result of the information that has obviously been generated through the work of Professor Lawler and his team?

Prof. Lawler : I might ask the CMO to comment. I don't know.

Senator RUSTON: I'm interested in understanding how this plays into an improvement in screening for Asherman's for women with fertility issues and how that actually plays in to the role of IVF.

Dr Noja : I might just add that in late last year we did write to all the colleges and alert them to the importance of looking at Asherman's syndrome and the potential impacts of sharp curettes and other intrauterine treatments. We provided that information and let them know that we were looking at it and reminded them of the RANZCOG guidance in relation to this.

Prof. Kidd : I've actually been communicating with the President of RANZCOG since the discussion earlier in the day. I think we'll need to go to RANZCOG and just get some more definitive advice for you.

Senator RUSTON: I'm more than happy to wait because it's obviously a very important issue. It would be good if it were able to be provided with that because it strikes me that there's a bit of a disconnect around all these particular issues and then you end up with a woman seeking to become a mother and being challenged by all of the implications from what's happened before. So it would be fantastic if you can come back with that. Thanks.

CHAIR: Senator Roberts, we'll return to you.

Senator ROBERTS: I'd like to ask questions of the interim CDC briefly, then the National Health and Medical Research Council briefly and then the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare. Thank you for being here tonight. I refer to an answer by Ms Wood in the December 2025 estimates regarding the potential research function of the CDC. Your answer was very carefully worded. You said:

The CDC won't be … conducting research on matters that are in the remit of other organisations. The CDC is a complement to the Commonwealth public health capability. It will not be taking over or otherwise leaning in on research conducted by any other Commonwealth entities …

That's not a no. Can I have a clear answer, please? Will the CDC be conducting research or causing research to be conducted—yes or no?

Mr McCormack : One of the functions for the CDC in our legislation is to advise on research requirements specifically as they relate to public health matters. We will be undertaking that, and we're therefore an active participant in research. We are not researchers ourselves in the sense of producing primary evidence, though we are an expert organisation, and we would expect a number of our staff, through the course of their work, to be participating in research undertaken cooperatively with institutions such as universities et cetera. But we're also not a significant funder of research. The principal funding mechanism for medical research in Australia is, of course, the NHMRC, complemented by programs administered by the department, including the Medical Research Future Fund. It's not a question that necessarily provides for a very simple yes-or-no answer. It's a bit of yes and a bit of no. We're a participant. We're not a principal researcher. We're a supporter of research strategy. We're not a significant funder of research.

Senator ROBERTS: You'll be participating in research, but you're not researching.

Mr McCormack : It's not a simple yes-or-no thing.

Senator ROBERTS: That's right. I understand.

Mr McCormack : We have a role in research under our legislation, but it's not to be a prime driver of research.

Senator ROBERTS: You haven't got hold of the beakers and the test tubes.

Mr McCormack : We do not have hold of the beakers and test tubes. No.

Senator ROBERTS: A further part of that answer was that the Gene Technology Standing Committee oversees gain-of-function research through the Office of the Gene Technology Regulator. The standing committee has not met since 2023, and their website was last updated in 2024. The website of the Office of the Gene Technology Regulator does not mention gain-of-function research. The only time they have interceded on the topic was for medical research, where they defended and approved the application. I'm pursuing this line of questioning because gain-of-function research gave the world the MERS virus and the COVID virus. President Obama banned gain-of-function research funding in 2014 owing to lab mishaps with anthrax, smallpox and avian flu. Every time I ask this government about this topic, I get an evasive answer. The Office of the Gene Technology Regulator just approved a public trial of gain-of-function research that produced an influenza virus replica. Australia is doing gain-of-function research, and the regulator is approving it. Minister, will this government ban gain-of-function research?

Senator Green: I don't have anything to add to answers that, I assume, have been given to you over many estimates and the information given by the officials tonight.

Senator ROBERTS: You won't. One Nation would ban—will ban—gain-of-function research.

Senator Green: It's great to hear about your policies, because then we know exactly what the Liberal-National policies will be in a few months.

Senator ROBERTS: We have been setting the agenda. Could I turn to the National Health and Medical Research Council, please. In 2025, the National Health and Medical Research Council funded the Vaccine Adjuvant Discovery and Development Centre of Research Excellence—CRE—led by Professor Katherine Andrews at Griffith University, with $5 million as part of a $72 million CRE package. This grant focuses on discovering new adjuvants to enhance vaccine efficacy, safety and related purposes. First question: Why do we need new adjuvants? What's wrong with the existing adjuvants?

Prof. Wesselingh : We assess grants through a peer review process. Through that process, we utilise experts from around Australia to assess all of the grants that come to us—whether it's for a centre of research excellence, an investigator grant or an ideas grant. The way that CRE would've been assessed would've been through that peer review process. Through that peer review process, they would've been elevated to the top of that scheme and would've been funded on the basis of their peers indicating that this was high-quality research that was likely to have a significant impact on health in Australia. We would take that on board; therefore, if they were ranked accordingly, we would fund them.

Senator ROBERTS: So you don't know the reasons why their peers elevated it to No. 1?

Prof. Wesselingh : I would have to go back and look at all of the assessments by those peers. Obviously, I don't have that directly in front of me at the moment.

Senator ROBERTS: Could you do that on notice, please? We'd like to know why that research was approved, why we need new adjuvants, and what's wrong with the existing adjuvants?

Prof. Wesselingh : I'm very happy to look back at the peer review. But what I can guarantee you is that they would have been regarded as excellent research likely to produce significant impact.

Senator ROBERTS: I'd like to know what they are.

Prof. Wesselingh : Sure.

Senator ROBERTS: Thank you. Adjuvants and vaccines are there to enhance the body's immune response to the antigen. Common adjuvants include aluminium hydroxide, aluminium phosphate, amorphous aluminium hydroxyphosphate sulphate and potassium aluminium sulphate. These have been widely linked to neurological conditions spontaneously occurring after vaccination. Is this program an admission that there might be a level of truth to the link between aluminium in vaccines and autism? I guess you wouldn't know, because you don't know the—

Prof. Wesselingh : So you're asking us if the fact that we funded the CRE is an admission? We, again, funded the CRE on the basis of the scores that the CRE obtained. Those scores would indicate the quality of the science and the likelihood of obtaining high-quality evidence to improve the health of Australians.

Senator ROBERTS: Right, and you're going to find the reason anyway, so perhaps you could check if there is any aspect of truth to the link between aluminium in vaccines and autism as part of the reasons for developing a new adjuvant?

Prof. Wesselingh : We can certainly look at the arguments that the CRE made and the peer review of that CRE.

Senator ROBERTS: Thank you. If research is successful and you find an effective adjuvant that is not neurotoxic, who will own the intellectual property the taxpayers just funded?

Prof. Wesselingh : The way our granting system works is that the intellectual property developed by—the people who get the grants from us, which are normally medical research institutes or universities or members of those organisations, own the intellectual property. So the intellectual property would be assigned according to a university's intellectual property rules or a medical research institute's rules. I'm not sure, with that CRE, where they were.

Senator ROBERTS: A $5 million synergy grant was awarded in 2024 to a multi-institutional team, including Monash University, to optimise vaccines for respiratory viruses, like influenza and RSV. This includes evaluating safety profiles to improve protection while minimising risks. If that develops new technology which achieves that objective, who will own that IP?

Prof. Wesselingh : Again, the IP would be organised according to the rules developed by the organisations as part of that synergy grant. Synergy grants tend to have a number of organisations from around Australia, so I imagine there are multiple universities and MRIs involved in that synergy grant, and they will have developed an IP policy and the IP will be owned according to that policy.

Senator ROBERTS: But not by the Australian government?

Prof. Wesselingh : Not by NHMRC or by the government.

Senator ROBERTS: We're very concerned about the level of spending in this government. Professor Bette Liu from the National Centre for Immunisation Research and Surveillance received a $2.79 million investigator grant in 2024 to study adult vaccination programs. This explicitly includes assessing vaccine safety, identifying risks in high-risk groups and informing safer program designs. What was the outcome of that grant?

Prof. Wesselingh : Again, if I knew the outcomes of all of the grants that I fund—we fund a billion dollars worth of grants every year—I think I'd be pretty good. I can't tell you the outcome of that grant, but we can take that on notice.

Senator ROBERTS: But you still think you're pretty good?

Prof. Wesselingh : Do I think I'm personally pretty good or the NHMRC is very good?

Senator ROBERTS: Both! Okay, thank you very much. I won't hold it against you for not answering. My question is to the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare. The Cancer data in Australia 2025 report emphasises that cancers, including breast cancer, are being diagnosed more frequently in people in their 30s and 40s, with the share of all breast cancer diagnoses rising about 50 per cent over the last 20 years, which is stunning. Breast cancer is now the most commonly diagnosed cancer for women aged 20 to 39 and 40 to 59, which is surprising as well. Have you undertaken any analysis to cross-reference breast cancer in this younger cohort with lifestyle factors—drinking, prescription medications and so on?

Dr Bolevich : We do indeed produce the report you're talking about and have a unit within the institute that specialises in cancer data—its collection, national consistency around it and various types of analysis. We often make the data available to researchers. For the specific question you're asking, I will defer to my colleague.

Ms Gates : As you said, we produce that information about cancer. We sometimes look at lifestyle factors. Specifically, it depends on what information we have around the connection between having a lifestyle factor, such as risk factors around smoking or other risk factors—I haven't got to hand anything directly that we've done in relation to breast cancer.

Senator ROBERTS: Could you take it on notice, to give us a range of what you provide in terms of lifestyle factors like drinking, prescription medications and so on?

Dr Bolevich : We can take that on notice.

Senator ROBERTS: We'd just like to see what you've got available; thank you. The American Cancer Society call this 'early onset breast cancer'. Specifically, have you cross-referenced breast cancer in this younger cohort with COVID vaccination status?

Dr Bolevich : No, we haven't done that kind of work.

Senator ROBERTS: Why not?

Dr Bolevich : I think we have provided updates to this committee on previous occasions about the work we've done to create some data infrastructure that will enable various types of research to occur. That infrastructure is now largely in place, and we would expect that over time people will undertake various types of analyses using that data and other data that's available to them. But the institute itself has not undertaken that specific type of research.

Senator ROBERTS: You're more the constructor of the database and the ability to cross-reference, but it will be up to someone else who wants to do that to do it?

Ms Hermann : Cancer Australia is undertaking a piece of work at the moment, directed by the minister, to look at the impacts of early onset cancer, including looking at lifestyle factors and other factors that may be influencing earlier rates of cancer in Australia.

Senator ROBERTS: What about COVID vaccination status?

Ms Hermann : I don't think that's included in what they're looking at.

Senator ROBERTS: I'm surprised, given what's in the public domain about that. Have you cross-referenced COVID vaccination status with any health outcome and any demographic?

Ms Gates : We have looked at vaccination status in terms of rates and that sort of thing, but, no, we haven't looked at that in terms of any associations.

Senator ROBERTS: I'm surprised, because of the news that's travelling around about that, including from many scientists. COVID injections were the most significant health response in Australian history, coming at a significant cost to the taxpayer and involving a significant level of coercion which, in hindsight, was not justified by the risk. The news about AstraZeneca and even the Pfizer shots, and the concerns, came out very early. There's a widely-held belief that the vaccines caused adverse events, and nothing but denials has come from the government—and not just this government but the previous government as well. If you have nothing to hide, Minister, why are you not doing the research which would confirm or disprove the link between COVID vaccination and adverse events, which would put a lot of people at ease?

Senator Green: The department and the officials have explained to you that there is work being undertaken on a range of research projects that look into trends in health care. Whether or not that's post COVID-19, there's a lot of time still to go before we see what that research might be. But the systems are being set up, and I'm sure that if there are any updates they'll give them to you first and foremost.

Senator ROBERTS: That's most unlike you, Minister, because it sounds like a lot of fluff. Is your government afraid of confirming that COVID shots cause early onset cancer? To me, people who have got cancer have got that thought in their mind; it's right through the community. People are worried, and if there is no connection it would be wonderful to take that off their burden. It sounds like, 'Bugger the people; just get on with the job and keep hiding it.'

Senator Green: I think the most important thing to do is to listen to the experts.

Senator ROBERTS: And common sense and what people in the street are saying.

Senator Green: And the health experts—particularly the health experts.

Senator ROBERTS: This is a short paragraph from your website on suicide:

Although males are more likely to die by suicide, females are hospitalised for intentional self-harm (with and without suicidal intent) almost twice as frequently as males … Furthermore, ambulance attendance data reporting on attendances for suicide attempts … suggest females are more likely to attempt suicide than males.

This is a very difficult topic, but is it any wonder that men kill themselves when this is how our health authorities minimise male suicides? Why are you conflating two different medical conditions—suicide and attention-seeking—to minimise the fact that men are three times more likely to successfully commit suicide than women? Surely we have to get the truth out there.

Senator Green: Sorry, did you just refer to self-harm as attention-seeking?

Senator ROBERTS: That's quite often what it's labelled.

Senator Green: I just wanted to get that on the record—that a One Nation senator is referring to self-harm as attention-seeking.

Senator ROBERTS: And quite often that's what psychiatrists will tell you.

Senator Green: I'm always shocked by the way you speak about women and their health care.

Senator ROBERTS: What's the answer to the question? Why are males committing suicide at three times the rate of women, yet we're conflating the issue?

Mr Comley : The AIHW can comment, but I don't think the quote you've read out is conflating the issue. It's talking about different prevalence rates of attempted suicide or attempted self-harm and what the consequences of that are. That seems to me a pretty straight factual statement that compares the impact on two genders of the patterns of reported outcomes and behaviour. I would not accept the premise of your question.

Senator ROBERTS: Thank you.

CHAIR: We are in a position now to release some more witnesses from this hearing. The Australian Centre for Disease Control, the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare and the National Health and Medical Research Council are all free to go. Senator Antic, you have the call.

Senator ANTIC: I've got some questions for the TGA. There's a range of topics here but I want to start with this one. An advertisement for a website called Know and Go has been sent to me; I can tender it. It says: 'One in four Aussies are at risk of severe COVID. Know if you're eligible for antiviral medicines and take the two-minute quiz.' It appears to be promoted by Pfizer, a pharmaceutical company. The Therapeutic Goods Act and the Advertising Code are some of the strictest advertising laws in the world, including a clear prohibition on advertising of prescription only medicines to the general public. What does the TGA think of ads like that? Does that cause any concern for the Therapeutic Goods Administration? They've been spotted on billboards and buses. There's a website. The question posed by this is determining people's eligibility for COVID-19 antiviral medicines which Pfizer makes.

Prof. Lawler : As you highlight, we do have very clear regulations and expectations around the advertising of prescription medicines and therapeutic goods, as governed by the Therapeutic Goods Act and also the regulations. We do take each case on its merits because it can often be quite nuanced—whether it's the medicine itself or a health service being advertised or whether there is an encouragement to seek appropriate assessment rather than direct access to a medicine. I have with me colleagues who are from our regulatory practice and support and regulatory compliance branches.

Mr Bedford : I might start and then Ms Lutton can add anything additional. As Professor Lawler has outlined—I'd like to have a look at the ad that you're referring to, because there are strict rules around the advertising of prescription medicines.

Senator ANTIC: This website, this advertising campaign, is not something that's currently on the TGA's radar for investigation, as far as you're aware?

Ms Lutton : I've only just received this advertisement, so I won't comment on this one specifically, but the TGA continues to actively monitor online content for potentially unlawful advertising of therapeutic goods and partner with several digital platforms to identify and address alleged breaches when they occur. For your awareness, over the 2024-25 financial year, we actually removed over 13,700 unlawful advertisements, including whole profiles from digital platforms and sites.

In 2024-25 we continue to expand that piece of work, particularly working with digital platform providers, including major online retailers, to identify and remove the unlawful advertisements. We work with several platforms with regard to those removals, but we also use our powers under section 313 of the Telecommunications Act, particularly where some of those websites are international—I haven't had a look at this website, particularly, to comment—where Australia has no jurisdiction. That will compel those ISPs, or internet service providers, to reroute that consumer or that purchaser back to the TGA website.

Senator ANTIC: This is an Australian site.

Prof. Lawler : I will highlight my understanding of this website. I'm not in the position of defending a process that's undertaken by a private company—

Senator ANTIC: I'm not suggesting there's anything wrong with it. I just want to know whether or not there's been a—

Prof. Lawler : My understanding—and again, I'll be happy to correct this if it's incorrect—is that it assesses on the basic eligibility that is used by our guidelines for access to antivirals. If you don't meet those then you're found to be not eligible. If you do meet those, you are directed to a healthcare professional. You're directed to a GP.

Senator ANTIC: On the subject of advertising in the pharmaceutical industry—it's always struck me that, as we've said, advertising prescription medicine is illegal in Australia, but there is no equivalent for over-the-counter medicines, which of course are owned by many of the same companies. The pharma market in Australia is something like $10 billion per annum. I don't know exactly what the over-the-counter market represents, but it's perhaps something like 10 or 20 per cent of that market, so pharmaceutical companies are, by definition, still pumping a lot of money into the media. Does that not give cause for concern when the media are reporting on health awareness campaigns, which may well drive pharmaceutical sales? There has to be a clear conflict of interest there, does there not?

Prof. Lawler : I appreciate that question. The regulations around advertising are very particular in Australia. Having seen the way in which medicines can be advertised fairly broadly overseas, I think that that drives demand in a way that is not necessarily well informed and not necessarily informed by interaction with a health professional. I think it is important to note that, as with many of the other decisions that we make, the approach that is taken for the restrictions around advertising is risk based. One of the reasons that that there are restrictions around prescription based medicines is that these are medicines that have been determined by one of our delegates in approving and scheduling that these can only be provided in consultation with an authorised prescriber. So these are medicines that already have been preselected of to be of higher risk. They carry with them potentially greater benefit but certainly higher risk. That's why prescription medicines are prohibited from being advertised.

Senator ANTIC: But the fact remains, doesn't it, that, if media companies are obtaining a significant revenue stream from pharmaceutical companies, they're less likely to be critical of potential problems that arise with these therapies and therapeutics. Would you say there not any call for a tightening of that such that there is no revenue stream into the media which might cause a natural reaction for the media to avoid criticising companies, their parent companies or the makers of other medications? They are the same companies—

Prof. Lawler : I understand the point entirely. I'm not really sufficiently expert to make comments on the decision process for media. I guess it does come down to a lot of the decisions that we make being decisions that are being made by other parts of the medicine supply chain, which is that these are medicines of a lower risk type and that individuals need to be aware of the availability to gain the benefit. As I said, we work through the regulations that we have, and they apply most particularly to prescription medicines but also to some other issues such as prohibited representations.

Senator ANTIC: Okay. Can I ask you about specifically about the flu vaccines. Pre COVID in Australia, there were an estimated 300 to 1,000 yearly flu deaths, according to statistical models. They're mixed in with some other respiratory illnesses, like pneumonia. A recent preprint study from the Cleveland Clinic tracked about 53,000 employees during the 2024-25 flu season. They had an 82 per cent vaccination rate, and it was found that vaccine hadn't been effective in preventing influenza. In fact, it found that flu cases were actually higher among the vaccinated than the unvaccinated. Flu coverage in Australia among Australians 65 and over rose from 25 per cent in 2000 to 75 per cent in 2019, and flu related deaths have gone from 300 to 500 annually in the early 2000s to 953 deaths in 2019. If these influenza vaccines are effective, why have rising vaccination rates not been accompanied by a clear reduction in winter illness mortality, particularly among the older, to whom they're targeted? And, first of all, is that correct? Are those are those statistics correct.

Prof. Gibney : Could you repeat the statistics?

Senator ANTIC: Probably the most concerning one is that flu vaccine coverage among Australians aged 65 and over rose from 25 per cent in 2000 to 75 per cent in 2019 but deaths have risen from 300 to 500 in the early 2000s to about 953 in 2019, which would suggest that the vaccination is not actually achieving the goals it was designed for.

Prof. Lawler : One quick thing: I think it's really important that a more comprehensive answer just on the statistics themselves might be taken on notice. There are going to be a lot of factors that are occurring alongside. These are not trends, if verified, that have occurred in isolation. Over the time period you're discussing, we have had, for instance, if I have it correct, the COVID pandemic, and so we're going to see some vaccination rates increase anyway.

Senator ANTIC: That blocked out a few years, but the trend is just significantly higher for flu rate. This is the National Communicable Disease Surveillance Dashboard, which shows a significant increase in flu cases. How does that overlay with a rollout of the vaccine program?

Prof. Gibney : I think it's really important that we understand the data and the statistics that you are referring to. One of the things about flu and surveillance data in Australia—or anywhere—is that it's really difficult to get accurate information about flu deaths using surveillance data, so I think we probably need to—

Senator ANTIC: Sorry to interrupt, but why is that?

Prof. Gibney : It is because the notifiable diseases are notified at diagnosis and we don't always get the outcome of the illness.

Senator ANTIC: We could tell how many people died of COVID in 10½ milliseconds, apparently, during COVID. We can't tell the same for the flu?

Prof. Gibney : Well, during COVID, there was a lot of follow up of notifications and a lot of work went into understanding outcomes. I'm not saying that there is no good data on flu deaths, but we just have to really understand the data that you're quoting and whether it's consistent.

Senator ANTIC: Not looking at my data—what does your data say about the increase in vaccination for the flu versus the increase the rates of death and flu related cases over a similar period? Let's say the last 10 years.

Prof. Gibney : What I can say is that we have data on the effectiveness of flu vaccine in preventing hospitalisations. It's the most robust data we have, and that is published every year. The flu vaccine isn't perfect by any stretch of the imagination, but it does prevent a range—around 50 per cent or more—of hospitalisations amongst vaccinated individuals, which is why we recommend flu vaccine and why it's funded for older Australians.

Senator ANTIC: What are the risks associated with it?

Prof. Gibney : With flu vaccination? Well, through the assessments of TGA and ATAGI, we can definitively say that the benefits outweigh the risks. All—

Senator ANTIC: How?

Prof. Gibney : By preventing many more hospitalisations than would be associated with the delivery of the vaccine.

Senator ANTIC: Well, what if you've had a serious adverse reaction to one? What then?

Prof. Gibney : Well, then, obviously the advice would be that you talk to your healthcare provider about an individual assessment of the event, its association with the vaccine and whether the risks and benefits of vaccine for that individual—where that lands.

Prof. Lawler : I would highlight, if I may, that the analysis of effectiveness is predominantly on a population level. So it's quite reasonable for you to ask, 'What about an individual as an adverse reaction?' The reason is because the benefit-risk that we talk about is at a population level. That goes to the general immunity. It goes to the reduction in the amount of hospitalisation and a reduction in deaths. The risk-benefit analysis for the person who has the adverse reaction is different, but you cannot know that prospectively. It's very similar to the fact that the benefit-risk ratio for the individual who is infected with influenza or with COVID or with polio or measles is also different to the population risk-benefit of vaccination.

Senator ANTIC: One of the concerns is the difficulty people have in reporting. I think that's always been one of the criticisms of the reporting system: that it's too difficult to report reactions. So that will only happen in the case of severe reactions. Can I just turn—how much time have I got left, Chair?

CHAIR: Sorry, Chair. I could make you the chair, Senator Antic!

Senator ANTIC: That was very unkind, sorry! I was just wondering how much time I have left for another—

CHAIR: Well, you can take as much time as you need. We're not cutting you off at this point. Do you need much longer?

Senator ANTIC: I've just got another thing. I'm happy to flip it around, but I've got some more after that. Can I do another—

CHAIR: Five minutes?

Senator ANTIC: Yes.

Prof. Lawler : I would just reflect very quickly on one comment you said. One of the things that I've discussed with you and also with other senators is that there's a large volume of adverse event reports for COVID vaccines. We've seen that. The reason for that is because we have, as much as possible, made the reporting process easier. The reason for that is that the validity of our postmarketing vigilance relies on us being able to access those results. So we have a very large volume of very useful data on vaccines, which gives us an understanding of the spread of the types of adverse events.

Senator ANTIC: The criticism I hear is that the notification system is very difficult to navigate and very difficult and not fruitful in the case of smaller and minor adverse reactions. By the way, we have been asking for that postmarketing vigilance for a significant period of time.

I want to turn my attention though to a different type—the pertussis vaccine in children. There was, I think, a Productivity Commission report a few weeks ago which claimed that Australia is in the middle of an escalating whooping cough outbreak. It's been reported all across the media that that is the case. Once again using the data from the national disease surveillance system—it shows actually that whooping cough notifications peaked in 2024 at around 57,000 cases and fell to about 25,000 in 2025, indicating that the peak has already passed. Why, therefore, is the public messaging continuing to frame pertussis as a current and escalating outbreak when the data says otherwise? And does the department have anything to do to correct the ledger on that?

Prof. Gibney : I'm confirming that you're correct that the current outbreak peaked in 2024, but cases are still very elevated. The reasons include the fact that pertussis is cyclical, so we always had peaks every three to four years pre COVID. Then there was a bigger gap during COVID because there was less transmission of everything, essentially, and then we had a lot of people who were didn't have natural immunity or had not been exposed to pertussis and had been vaccinated. It just left a bit of an immunity gap and so we had more pertussis post-COVID in this wave, but that is now reducing.

Senator ANTIC: So would it be fair, then, for the department to notify our friends in the media that we are not currently at the highest watermark? Is there not an obligation on the department to do that? A lot of mothers would be particularly concerned about hearing that misinformation. We don't like misinformation.

Prof. Kidd : We are still concerned about pertussis rates.

Senator ANTIC: Of course.

Prof. Kidd : We're always concerned about cases of whooping cough, particularly those affecting infants under the age of two months who have not been able to be vaccinated. Those children, of course, are at risk if older siblings or older children who they may come in contact with acquire pertussis and infect them.

Senator ANTIC: Sure. Some of these news organisations are reporting—and I quote; I won't name the outlet—the 'highest levels of whooping cough since records began 30 years ago'. I know it's not your position to deal with the media, but the media are saying this. Why doesn't the department therefore correct the ledger and make it perhaps a little less concerning for parents who might be worried about that specific fact? I'm not suggesting it isn't out in the community, but it is not accurate to say that at this point it's at its highest peak in the last 30 years.

Prof. Gibney : I would say that pertussis levels are still very high, so, as to the public health messaging that that childhood vaccination and maternal vaccination are important, that is still the case.

Senator ANTIC: Just on the subject of that being important and the risks in particular associated with this particular vaccine, we've been through this before, but I presume this also hasn't had a placebo controlled test. There are different versions.

Prof. Lawler : We have responded to those questions.

Senator ANTIC: I have perhaps one or two more. Can the department provide year-by-year data on pertussis/whooping cough related hospitalisations and severe outcomes from 2022 to 2025, and is there any explanation as to why these numbers are not readily available and prioritised for public communications, which would achieve the outcome that I suggested, which is that the ledger about the peaking levels should be correct?

Dr Peatt : We'd have to take that question on notice. I don't have those figures in front of me, but we can provide you that later.

Senator ANTIC: Alright. Does the. pertussis vaccine prevent infection or transmission?

Prof. Gibney : The pertussis vaccine protects against severe disease. It's not the best vaccine. It's the second time I've said that in answer to your questions, in short. You can see that by the fact that we give five vaccines during childhood and another dose in adolescence on the NIP and then recommend at least another two doses during adulthood. That's aside from the maternal vaccines.

Senator ANTIC: It's a big payday for pharma, isn't it—getting seven doses or whatever it is.

Dr Peatt : If I may just add, it is a vaccine that does provide protection, but the antibodies that are produced by the body in response to the vaccination wane over time. Without those vaccines, the community would be at greater risk from pertussis.

Senator ANTIC: But, to be clear, this vaccine does not prevent infection or transmission. That is the answer. I understand the arguments about severe disease and hospitalisation, but it is possible, is it not, for those who are inoculated to carry the disease, spread it and not even know they have it, perhaps, because of the dampening of the disease?

Prof. Gibney : I would have to take that on notice.

Prof. Lawler : I would say, if I may, just a couple of things. It is possible for that to occur, which is why we encourage, where possible, the highest level of vaccination.

Senator ANTIC: So the vaccine doesn't work, so we've got to then give it to everyone.

Prof. Lawler : No.

Prof. Gibney : The vaccine does work.

CHAIR: Let Professor Lawler finish his answer.

Prof. Lawler : I understand that it's attractive to represent the vaccine as not working, but that's not—

Senator ANTIC: Well, we need seven of them.

Prof. Lawler : As you yourself have agreed—well, not agreed but acknowledged—the vaccine is very important for the prevention of severe infection or death.

Senator ANTIC: I don't think I said that. I'm just asking the questions here.

Prof. Lawler : It is vitally important that we recognise, particularly in the instance of transmission, that we do try and maintain vaccination rates as high as they can be. On your other question, around whether it's a placebo studied vaccine, we did respond to that in SQ25001578.

Senator ANTIC: That's good. You've been on WhatsApp. Excellent.

Prof. Lawler : No. I have the record of when we responded to your question.

Senator ANTIC: I have a final question on this subject. If it doesn't stop infection or transmission or have an effect on herd immunity, the question that's of interest to me is: why are we forcing grandparents to be vaccinated before they can see their grandchildren if it is, as we have acknowledged, not one of the best—or whatever the words were—vaccines? Why are we forcing grandparents to do that?

Prof. Gibney : I would say that there's no forcing of grandparents to have vaccines. It is in the Australian Immunisation Handbook that people who live with, care for or have contact with infants who are too young to be vaccinated consider being vaccinated. But, really, the main drive and the thing that makes the most difference is providing direct protection, which is through maternal vaccination, so that the young babies have antibodies in the first few months of life and then childhood vaccination, which begins at six weeks. That is what protects babies from hospitalisation and death from pertussis.

Senator RUSTON: I have a few questions, following on from Senator Liddle, in relation to the National Mental Health and Suicide Prevention Agreement. I think I'm asking my own question. Can the department confirm that the Commonwealth has offered the states and territories a one-year extension on the National Mental Health and Suicide Prevention Agreement?

Dr Develin : That's correct.

Senator RUSTON: Have all of the states and territories accepted the offer?

Dr Develin : It is my understanding that five states so far have signed the agreement.

Senator RUSTON: Which states are they?

Mr Matthews : The ones that have not signed are the ACT, Victoria and New South Wales.

Senator RUSTON: I thought you said five.

Mr Matthews : Yes, there are five. The three that have not signed are the ACT—

Senator RUSTON: Oh, so they're the three that haven't signed.

Mr Matthews : It's probably easier to run through the three.

Senator RUSTON: There are couple of quite big ones.

Mr Matthews : Yes, there are a couple of big ones. The message is that they're working through their processes to confirm agreement to the extension.

Senator RUSTON: Is it still the intent that the new three-year agreement will commence in July 2026 or July 2027?

Dr Develin : The extension is for the 2026-27 year period.

Senator RUSTON: At the end of 2027, this one-year extension finishes. Is the intention that there will be a three-year agreement post that or is that still up in the air?

Dr Develin : That is very much a live discussion of health and mental health ministers. We actually have a health and mental health ministers meeting on Friday. We have had sector consultation and discussions between governments that there would be intention for a future agreement, but that will be, of course, subject to government decision-making.

Senator RUSTON: The Productivity Commission findings in its recent report suggested, or recommended, the re-establishment of the Mental Health Commission and the National Suicide Prevention Office. In your awareness, is that being considered as part of the new agreement?

Dr Develin : That is really a matter for the Commonwealth government as opposed to an intergovernmental agreement with the states and territories because the commission is fully funded, and had previously been established, under Commonwealth legislation. The Commonwealth government is considering that. I think we have been pretty clear that it is an interim arrangement, but it is sitting within the department, and the government—

Senator RUSTON: What is an interim arrangement?

Dr Develin : The move of the National Mental Health Commission, which is currently sitting within the department as a temporary arrangement, while the government considers its future governance arrangements.

Senator RUSTON: Minister?

Senator Green: I can't add to what the officials have said. I think it's under consideration at the moment.

Senator RUSTON: So will you take that on notice?

Senator Green: Yes, I can take it on notice. Absolutely, I can ask the minister. It's probably a bit late for me to try to get back to you tonight, but we'll certainly try to get that to you as quickly as possible.

Mr Matthews : What would also add to that is that the role—while that decision on how that commission is formed and where it sits would be for the Commonwealth, the role of the commission in the national agreement, in terms of reporting, as you know they do the performance reports et cetera for it now, so the role of the commission in a future national agreement would be something that we would negotiate with the states and territories.

Senator Green: Just to clarify, what I meant by 'it's under consideration' is the way that it's established. We are committed to establishing it.

Senator RUSTON: Fine. I don't know whether the department knows this, or if it's another one for you, Minister, but is the government intending to formally respond to the PC report and its recommendations?

Dr Develin : We don't have a sense from government in terms of responding to the report. It was commissioned by governments about the previous agreement, and hence any response would effectively be, 'What is the next future agreement,' because the PC report was very much to inform that. We anticipate the largest mechanism of response will really be the design of any future agreement, as opposed to a response that might go line by line through the recommendations.

Mr Matthews : Any formal response to the agreement, given that it's a Commonwealth-state agreement, would realistically probably require a collective response of all the jurisdictions in one go. It wouldn't be that the Commonwealth would necessarily respond on its own. As Ms Develin said, the response will effectively be the negotiation of the new agreement.

Senator RUSTON: Okay. Just quickly, before I hand back to others, in the National suicide prevention strategy2025-2035, there was an ambition for the reduction of suicide rates, which obviously every single person would want to see. I'm keen to understand what is the specific numerical reduction in suicide deaths the government is aiming for under the National Suicide Prevention Strategy. It did not seem to be there, unless I've misread it.

Dr Develin : I don't believe we've set targets—

Senator RUSTON: There are no targets?

Dr Develin : or forecast for future suicide rates in Australia. As you would appreciate, it's a devastating thing for families, but it's still a relatively small number of incidents each year. While each one is completely devastating, they are small incidences each year. It does move around, because it is such a small number. It does fluctuate. The government has not set a target for the future.

Senator RUSTON: 'Small numbers'?

Dr Develin : Small numbers in terms of the numbers of suicide.

Senator RUSTON: 'Small numbers'?

Dr Develin : In relation to other causes of death, in that sense, but, as I said, it is a devastating thing for any family to experience.

Senator RUSTON: So 3,307 Australians taking their lives is a 'small number'? With the greatest of respect, Dr Develin, I'm not sure I would consider that a small number of people who have taken their own life.

Dr Develin : Senator, just to make sure everyone is perfectly clear on my comments, that is in relation to the other causes of death in Australia.

Senator RUSTON: Okay.

Mr Matthews : One other aspect to that, the National Suicide Prevention Office is also developing an outcomes framework to sit alongside the Suicide Prevention Strategy, which will partly be about how it looks to interpret the strategy from the point of view of: 'What does it do? What does it mean? What does it achieve?'

Senator RUSTON: I'm not sure too many parents who have lost a child are particularly worried about an outcomes framework, but, nonetheless, the funding package that was announced with the strategy included $69 million as a headline figure. How much of that has been spent to date?

Mr Matthews : I'll probably have to take it on notice how much has been spent, but certainly the majority of that has been through—a lot of that funding is through the national suicide prevention leadership program that is largely in contract. We could take that on notice to get you a figure of how much has been spent, but it would be under contract with our providers who are doing it. So we can, if you like, give you an update. There is a large number of actions underneath that funding.

Senator RUSTON: Sure. It would be great to know how much has been spent and how much is committed to be spent. As part of that information, can you get what are the measurable impacts that have been observed on things like suicide attempts and emergency department presentations? Obviously, the most important statistic of all is how that $69 million, or the measures that have made up much of that $69 million, has been spent in terms of the outcomes that have been achieved.

Mr Matthews : I would say that from a statistics point of view obviously there were I think 3,307 in 2024 and about 3,300 in the year before, so there's not a lot of variance between the two years from that point of view. But lots of the programs don't necessarily take a reduction in the suicide rate as their overall measure of success. There'll be a range of different things, whether they're prevention, education and or other things.

Senator RUSTON: But at the end of the day we want to stop people from attempting suicide. We want to stop people who attempt suicide who injure themselves actually requiring medical treatment, and most importantly we want to reduce and hopefully eliminate deaths. In terms of the metrics of how you measure what your deliverables are, they're really the bottom line in terms of what you're trying to deliver. I'd just be keen to know how much of the $69 million has been spent and what the measurement in terms of the impact of that has been on those things that are actually the outcomes that we're trying to measure. It's not about outputs and it's not about actions; it's actually about outcomes.

Mr Matthews : I think we understand that. I'm just probably flagging in the response to that that obviously what we fund is AIHW to do the data collection around that that provides the broader set of statistics, which of course we monitor and watch, but it's the attribution of the programs that we fund, which might be $500,000, $1 million or something like that. The attribution of that to a broader national dataset on either hospitalisations or suicide is probably tricky to get that attribution from that program to that. I think I understand what you're trying to do. We'll get you as far as we can in that answer.

Senator RUSTON: I understand, but it would be really nice to get some of these answers in retail speak: what does it mean to Australia? You've spent $69 million. What's it done for Australia? Finally, what are the top three cohorts where suicide rates are remaining the most stubborn or even potentially worsening, and what measures have been taken in relation to that? I'm just keen to understand: are there particular cohorts or target groups that you continue to focus on?

Mr Matthews : Statistically males are highly disproportionately flagged from that, so there are probably a range of different cohorts that we'd look at from that point of view.

Senator RUSTON: Do you break them down? Have you got a list?

Mr Matthews : The data is available, so it is possible from that. Obviously you can break it down by gender, you can break it down by age and there are different priority groups within that. I think it came up in one of the other questions on notice we had before around the types of occupations, and there is some work from that which helps us from a targeting point of view. Of course then there's a First Nations question, which is the one that is unfortunately still increasing that we talked about earlier. They would be the target groups.

Senator RUSTON: Can you just find a bit more data around this so we can understand where you're targeting the money and how it's working, because there's no point having a target to zero if we're not seeing any outcome.

Mr Matthews : Absolutely.
